A web search engine, like Google, often returns thousands of results for a simple query. For example, if you type the search term “jaguar” into Google, around 200 million results are returned. This makes it very difficult to browse or find relevant information, especially if the search term has multiple meanings. If we search for “jaguar”, we might be looking for information about the animal, the car, or the Jacksonville Jaguars football team. Clustering methods can be used to automatically group search results into categories, making it easier to find relavent results. This method is used in the search engines PolyMeta and Helioid, as well as on FirstGov.

Festivals are woven into the fabric of life throughout Latin America — from the Bolivian Altiplano and the Peruvian Andes to the far reaches of Easter Island. They’re events where communities come together to celebrate faith, heritage and identity, often blending Indigenous traditions with influences brought by European colonisers centuries ago. And for travellers, they’re an opportunity to experience local culture at its most vivid. Streets fill with music and dance, as performers parade through cities, towns and village squares, while age-old rituals are brought to life before cheering crowds. Here are seven of the best. 1. Originally an Indigenous festival of the Uru people, it centred on a pilgrimage to the sacred mountains surrounding Oruro, where participants prayed for protection from deities associated with toads, lizards and snakes. When the Spanish arrived, they blended these traditions with Christian beliefs, gradually shaping the modern-day Oruro Carnival. Its centrepiece is the Diablada — the Dance of Devils — during which revellers don elaborate demonic masks and costumes. Jesse McClary, Redux By Liz Brumer-Smith Published April 8, 2026 Nothing feels better than spending time outdoors after months of snow, grey skies, and frigid weather. Spring is a special season, no matter where you are, but in some areas of the country, the landscape blossoms to life with particular brilliance. Green overtakes the once barren trees, colorful wildflowers pop up in hills and valleys, and waterfalls rage from snowmelt. The north often takes longer to reach its peak season, but many state parks in the south and southwest are in their prime season from February to May. If you want a natural escape this spring, consider visiting one of these seven stunning state parks while they are ripe with beauty. ( Fifty of our favorite U.S. state parks .) 1. A self-drive safari can take many forms but at its heart is the irresistible idea that in being at the wheel in the midst of wildlife you’re briefly part of the ecosystem around you. You have an agency and freedom that only intensifies the thrill. At its most basic level, a self-drive simply involves hiring a 4WD from a car rental outfit, packing your own camping gear and heading towards the horizon. At a more advanced level, it can mean hiring a vehicle complete with all manner of equipment, such as a rooftop tent, kitchen, satellite phone and spare fuel cans for long-distance drives. In some places you’ll be able to drive your vehicle independently within national parks and private game reserves, camping within their boundaries using the gear you’ve carried. Texas’s second largest city is in the midst of a cultural revival, with the up-and-coming Pearl district leading the charge. A long-exposure photograph captures stars appearing to streak across the night sky above Joshua Tree National Park in California. Two meteor showers punctuate the month: The Draconids peak beneath the dark skies of a nearly new moon, while the Orionids arrive later in October. Saturn also reaches opposition, when the planet appears at its biggest and brightest, creating an excellent opportunity to glimpse its famed rings. Meteor showers—and, now that autumn has arrived, the northern lights —are best viewed beneath dark skies away from light pollution . Saturn at opposition — October 4 Saturn will reach its closest point to Earth, known as its opposition, around 8 a.m. ET on Oct. 4. There’s no better way to unzip a country than on foot, but the logistics of hiking often involve some serious forward planning — and often a solid amount of time in the driving seat. Not so with rail-to-trail hiking, which, thanks to Europe’s increasingly interconnected rail network, is having something of a moment, offering a remarkably hassle-free way to reach Europe’s wild places while allowing for even more time soaking up those dramatic landscapes. Pick your hike, catch the train first thing and you can be lacing up boots, slinging on a backpack and hitting the trail while most people are still polishing off breakfast. From half-day treks in the Swiss Alps to multi-day pilgrimages through Tuscany’s medieval hill towns, we’ve combed Europe to bring you eight of the best hikes you can tackle straight off the train carriage. Mexico City’s cocktail scene is distinguished by its imaginative use of native ingredients and regional spirits. Mexico City’s street food scene is world-renowned, from its dripping birria tacos to its overstuffed tamales, served steaming-hot from bustling stalls. But there’s another side to the Mexican hospitality experience, found under the moody lights of lavish speakeasies and well-stocked cocktail bars. Mexico City’s mixology has taken an inventive turn over the last few years as indigenous ingredients make their way into the spotlight. It’s not unfamiliar to taste pulque (fermented agave) as a natural sweetener or raicilla instead of the more widely known local spirit, tequila. These have long been a part of the Mexican cocktail experience — but, as Baltra Bar’s head bartender José Luis says, “what’s changed is the attention the world is now paying to it”. In Sweden, Midsummer shares the seasonal spotlight with the country's beloved crayfish parties. Food is central to travel: it gives us a flavour of a place, its customs and the people who live there. Yet, some of the most rewarding culinary experiences have nothing to do with restaurants. Food cultures and practices are shaped by the landscape, the seasons and generations of know-how, whether it's foraging in mountain forests or harvesting the fruit of ancient trees. And travellers can get involved, too, taking part in hands-on experiences that offer an insight into local traditions — from fermenting in Devon to catching crayfish in Sweden. Review 13 C.F.R. § 134 .404. OHA must receive your appeal by 5 p.m. ET on the 45th business day. Where to file We accept appeals by email at ohafilings@sba.gov . Appeals sent to other email addresses are not formal filings. We also accept appeals via the Hearing and Appeals Submission Upload (HASU) Application . Please note that submitting an appeal using HASU is not required and HASU is only used to transmit the appeal to OHA. Park Güell in Barcelona is one of famous architect Antoni Gaudí's most celebrated masterpieces. Anastasy Yarmolovich, Getty Images By Isabella Noble and Lauren Gamp Published July 1, 2026 This article was produced by National Geographic Traveller (UK). Celebrating the completion of the Sagrada Família this year, the Catalan capital has a rich creative heritage stretching back to medieval times, when crafts thrived among the tangled stone streets of what’s now Ciutat Vella (Old Town). Today, Barcelona’s best hotels blend a thoroughly Catalan character with a design-forward style. Ongoing bans on constructing new hotels in the city centre — introduced to help manage overtourism — mean there are few fully new openings. Instead, many stays have reinvented themselves with bold makeovers, imaginative cuisine and fresh services. Hotel Brummell stands out for its central location and rooftop pool. Coral Solari 1.
